title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
Problem (from the previous page, scribe Golovin, Adversaria I pp. 10-13, usually dated c. 1766): find two surfaces that can be carried one into the other so that corresponding points keep their mutual distances, i.e. two isometric (applicable) surfaces. On the previous page Euler writes the general conditions E=E', F=F', G=G' for parametrisations X(r,s), Y(r,s). He calls solving them by known methods 'maxime arduum' and switches to an ansatz.

The ansatz: X(r,s) = c(r) + s c'(r), where c'(r) = T(r) = (J,G,H), and likewise for the second surface with c'(r) = (L,M,N). This is exactly the tangent developable of a space curve c. Writing T' = dT/dr, we have X_r = T + sT' and X_s = T.
- Equating the coefficient of ds^2 gives |T|^2 = |T~|^2.
- Equating the dr ds coefficient gives T.(T+sT') = T~.(T~+sT~').
- Equating the dr^2 coefficient gives |T+sT'|^2 = |T~+sT~'|^2.
Collecting powers of s yields three conditions: |T|^2 = |T~|^2, T.T' = T~.T~', and |T'|^2 = |T~'|^2. The second follows from the first by differentiation.

Euler then sets |T| = p and writes T = p(sin m sin n, cos m sin n, cos n), i.e. spherical coordinates of the unit tangent, and likewise with angles mu, nu. Then |T'|^2 = p'^2 + p^2(sin^2 n m'^2 + n'^2). So the remaining condition is dm^2 sin^2 n + dn^2 = dmu^2 sin^2 nu + dnu^2.

In modern terms: p dr = d(sigma) is arclength of the edge of regression. The condition says the tangent indicatrices of the two curves have equal speed, i.e. the curves have the same curvature kappa(sigma) as a function of arclength, with torsion arbitrary. Euler parametrises the solution in two ways:
- choose m, n, nu freely and get dmu = sqrt(dm^2 sin^2 n + dn^2 - dnu^2)/sin nu;
- or introduce theta (the common indicatrix arclength, i.e. the integral of kappa d(sigma)) and get dm = sqrt(dtheta^2 - dn^2)/sin n and dmu = sqrt(dtheta^2 - dnu^2)/sin nu.
The explicit coordinates follow, with p an arbitrary function of r. Result: tangent developables of two curves with equal curvature function are isometric.

Adnotatio. The second surface cannot be prescribed (e.g. a sphere): r and s range to infinity, so these surfaces are unbounded, and no bounded figure such as a sphere is contained in the formulas. For closed surfaces Euler asserts that a solid figure closed on all sides admits no change, citing the regular bodies, so an entire sphere is rigid. Non-closed figures can change; a hemisphere is certainly mutable, but which deformations it admits is 'problema difficillimum' (next page).
errors: Euler's explanation of why a sphere is excluded (unboundedness of the parameter range) misses the real reason. His ansatz produces only tangent developables, which have Gaussian curvature zero and are all locally isometric to the plane. No piece of a sphere, bounded or not, can belong to the family. The family is thus far from general, and the 'solution' consists only of flat surfaces, which Euler does not remark.
Letting s run over all reals covers both sheets of the tangent developable, which meet along the cuspidal edge s=0. The parametrisation is singular there; this is not noted.

The rigidity assertion 'statim atque figura solida undique est clausa, nullam amplius mutationem patitur' is a conjecture, not a theorem. It holds for convex polyhedra (Cauchy 1813) and convex closed surfaces (Liebmann, Cohn-Vossen; global uniqueness of ovaloids). It is false for general closed polyhedra: Connelly's flexible polyhedron (1977).
Minor point: the square roots in dmu and dm require the radicands to be non-negative (real constraint); this is left implicit.

ideas.what: General formulation of isometric (applicable) surfaces via equality of the three first-fundamental-form coefficients
ideas.modern_name: Isometry of surfaces / first fundamental form E,F,G
ideas.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Disquisitiones generales 1827); Euler's E419 (1772) for developables; Minding 1839 for applicability
ideas.where_published: E419 'De solidis quorum superficiem in planum explicare licet' (Novi Comm. 16, 1772) uses similar conditions for the plane case

ideas.what: Ansatz X = c(r) + s c'(r) and reduction of isometry to equality of |c'| and |c''|, i.e. equal curvature as a function of arclength with torsion free
ideas.modern_name: Tangent developables of curves with equal curvature are isometric (bending of a curve's tangent surface)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical 19th-century differential geometry (Monge school; textbook result)
ideas.where_published: Related material in E419; this fragment is published in Opera postuma I (1862), pp. 494-496

ideas.what: Rigidity of closed surfaces (closed figure admits no change; the regular bodies as evidence); the whole sphere is rigid, the hemisphere is flexible
ideas.modern_name: Euler's rigidity conjecture; Cauchy rigidity theorem; Liebmann's sphere rigidity
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler 1766 (conjecture, quoted from exactly this fragment); Cauchy 1813; Liebmann 1899; counterexample Connelly 1977
ideas.where_published: This very passage (Opera postuma I, 494-496), widely quoted, e.g. Gluck 1975 and Connelly's papers

ideas.what: Spherical-coordinate parametrisation of the unit tangent, giving |T'|^2 = p'^2 + p^2(sin^2 n m'^2 + n'^2)
ideas.modern_name: Speed of the tangent indicatrix = curvature times arclength

missed.claim: Euler explicitly constructs the general family of isometric pairs of tangent developables, parametrised by an arbitrary common indicatrix length theta(r) and free angles. In effect this is the statement that a tangent developable can be bent by changing the torsion of its edge while keeping curvature, apparently decades before it became textbook. It is probably known to specialists in the history of rigidity/developables, but credit to Euler for this specific statement is rarely given.
missed.quote: introducto novo angulo θ functione ipsius r, tantum capi poterit dm = √(dθ²−dn²)/sin n et dμ = √(dθ²−dν²)/sin ν
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is minor historiographical credit for an early explicit bending construction. It is mathematically routine today.

deep.surprise_reason: The page's famous content, Euler's closed-surface rigidity conjecture, is well known and routinely cited to this exact fragment. The tangent-developable isometry construction is correct and early but mathematically standard. Its partial novelty is only a matter of attribution detail.
transcription_corrections: The machine transcription is essentially faithful to the image. Euler's 'J' corresponds to a Fraktur-style I in the print, consistent with the previous page. The occurrence printed as 'J^2+G^2+H^2=pp' in 'statuamus' is correct.
The two final coordinate systems are printed side by side in the image ('pro priori' and 'pro posteriori'); the transcription interleaves them correctly.
